paragraphs: Naturally Favorable to the Concentration of Power

The idea of secondary powers placed between the sovereign and his subjects came naturally to the imagination of aristocratic nations, because those communities contained individuals or families raised above the common level, apparently destined to command by their birth, their education and their wealth. For the opposite reasons, this same idea is naturally lacking in the minds of men in democratic ages. It can be introduced only artificially and kept there only with difficulty. By contrast, they conceive, almost without thinking about it, the idea of a single central power that governs the whole community by its direct influence. Moreover, in politics as in philosophy and religion, the intellect of democratic nations is particularly open to simple and general ideas. It dislikes complicated systems, and its favorite conception is that of a great nation made up of citizens who all resemble the same pattern and are all governed by a single power.

The idea that comes right after that of a single central power, in the minds of men in ages of equality, is the idea of uniformity of legislation. Every man sees that he differs little from those around him, so he cannot understand why a rule that applies to one man should not apply equally to all the others. The slightest privileges therefore offend his reason, the faintest differences in the political institutions of one people offend him, and uniformity of legislation seems to him the first condition of good government. I find, on the contrary, that this idea of a uniform rule, equally binding on all members of the community, was almost unknown to the human mind in aristocratic ages. It was either never entertained or rejected. These opposite tendencies of opinion eventually turn, on each side, into such blind instincts and such ungovernable habits that they still direct men’s actions in spite of particular exceptions. Conditions in the Middle Ages varied immensely, yet a certain number of persons at that time were in precisely similar circumstances. That did not stop the laws then in force from assigning each of them different duties and different rights. Today, on the contrary, all the powers of government are exerted to impose the same customs and the same laws on populations that as yet have few points of resemblance. As the conditions of men become equal among a people, individuals seem less important and society larger. Or rather, every citizen, being made like all the rest, is lost in the crowd, and nothing stands out but the great and imposing image of the people at large. This naturally gives the men of democratic periods a lofty opinion of the privileges of society and a very humble idea of the rights of individuals. They are ready to admit that the interests of the former are everything and those of the latter nothing. They are willing to grant that the power representing the community has far more information and wisdom than any of its members, and that it is the duty as well as the right of that power to guide as well as govern each private citizen.

If we examine our contemporaries closely and get down to the root of their political opinions, we will find some of the ideas I have just described. We may even be surprised to find so much agreement between men who are so often at odds. The Americans hold that in every State the supreme power ought to come from the people. But once that power is constituted, they can conceive, as it were, of no limits to it, and they are ready to admit that it has the right to do whatever it pleases. They have not the slightest idea of special privileges granted to cities, families or persons. It seems never to have crossed their minds that the same laws might not be applied with strict uniformity to every part of the country and to all its inhabitants. These same opinions are spreading more and more in Europe. They even creep in among those nations that most vehemently reject the principle of the sovereignty of the people. Such nations give a different origin to the supreme power, but they ascribe the same characteristics to it. Among all of them the idea of intermediate powers is weakened and wiped out. The idea of rights inherent in certain individuals is rapidly disappearing from men’s minds, and the idea of the omnipotence and sole authority of society at large rises to take its place. These ideas take root and spread as social conditions become more equal and men more alike. Equality produces them, and in turn they hasten the progress of equality.

In France, where the revolution I am speaking of has gone further than in any other European country, these opinions have taken complete hold of the public mind. If we listen attentively to the language of the various parties in France, we find that there is not one that has not adopted them. Most of these parties criticize the conduct of the government, but they all hold that the government ought to act perpetually and interfere in everything that is done. Even the parties most at odds agree on this point. The unity, the ubiquity and the omnipotence of the supreme power, and the uniformity of its rules, are the principal characteristics of all the political systems put forward in our age. They recur even in the wildest visions of political regeneration; the human mind pursues them in its dreams. If these ideas arise spontaneously in the minds of private individuals, they suggest themselves still more forcefully to the minds of princes. As the ancient fabric of European society is altered and dissolved, sovereigns acquire new conceptions of their opportunities and their duties. For the first time they learn that the central power they represent may and ought to administer, through its own agents and on a uniform plan, all the concerns of the whole community. I will venture to say that the monarchs of Europe never conceived this opinion before our time. Now it sinks deeply into the minds of kings and stays there amid all the agitation of more unsettled thoughts.

Our contemporaries are therefore much less divided than is commonly supposed. They dispute constantly over whose hands supremacy should be placed in, but they readily agree on the duties and rights of that supremacy. The idea they all form of government is that of a single, simple, providential and creative power. All secondary opinions in politics are unsettled; this one remains fixed, unchanging and consistent. Statesmen and political philosophers adopt it, and the multitude eagerly seizes it. Those who govern and those who are governed pursue it with equal ardor. It is the foremost idea in their minds, and it seems inborn. It therefore originates in no caprice of the human intellect but is a necessary condition of the present state of mankind.
